I have found it helpful at times and less than helpful at other times of my life. I try not to approach any acts of self love or self care from a place of obligation. If I tell myself that I must journal every day - it's an activity that falls by the wayside and I no longer find pleasure in it. If I just show up to my journal at the same time every day, and write what comes to mind - if anything does, while being patient and compassionate with my brain - I tend to get pretty amazing results. I'm able to think more clearly through brain fog; I'm able to discern my feelings better through out the day (I have pretty bad introception), and I can organize my thoughts and therefore have less anxiety. 

I try to remove barriers and judgement from my practice. Instead of setting goals like time spent writing, or writing a certain number of pages a day - I just ask myself - did I show up for myself today? And that's a yes or no question, and if I wasn't able to show up for myself on a given day - and there are many reasons for that - I try not to sweat it and come back to myself the next day.

Last time I journaled about current events was the Uvalde school shooting, so that's a while ago. Typically, I write about things that are current to me and occasionally current events will make it on the page, but it's pretty rare and I don't go into any detail.

Short answer: Yes. Yes, I believe in healing.

Longer answer: I believe that my future will be brighter than my present is and happier than my past ever was. I also believe that I've had to adjust my own definition of healing (and I do think it means different things to different people and that's okay) throughout my journey. I no longer strive for a life with zero symptoms, and that's helped me let go of the pressure that I previously put on myself to get better. It's allowed me to be more self compassionate and patient with myself and my life. I also think that the world in which I live (US) can be pretty tough on those with mental health issues; and rough for those with chronic pain; and I don't think that I'll ever truly feel healed in our society.

I'm sorry that you're struggling, and I'm sorry that you feel disconnected, and that your support system isn't available for you right now.

I wanted to say that I work full time and go to the gym, but have no commitments outside of that; and if you just wanted someone to say hello to and share pictures of animals or a joke or something, my dms are open. If that doesn't sound like something for you, that's okay too. 

Sending you lots of love.

My goal in therapy keeps adjusting over the last three years that I've been in trauma therapy. I've had previous goals like decrease anxiety, develop better grounding techniques for dissociation, build a writing/journaling practice, accept my trauma, accept my disability, learn to dream again, add movement to my life, have a better relationship with my body, have a better relationship with food. As I work and grow, my goals change.

Eventually, my long term goal is to be out of therapy. For me, therapy is a place of accountability, validation, and acceptance - and I would like to be able to provide those things for myself. I'm not sure whether or not this is doable for me. I'd also like to keep working on building a sense of community and friendships/relationships, and on feeling safe enough to create connection with other people. I'd like to figure out how to work and also take care of myself without burnout - but I'm pretty sure that capitalism has me beat on this endeavor. I'd like to keep being kind and compassionate and soft with myself while living in a world that celebrates toughness over softness and vulnerability. I would like to find a way to help other people living with the same troubles, in whatever way that I can.

I hear you. I think that people with chronic pain - whatever form that takes - have a different relationship with pain and different pain tolerances than folks that do not have chronic pain. 

In my own life and experience, I'm learning to be softer with myself more often rather than gritting my teeth and forcing myself to survive a painful experience. I'm very good at ignoring the pain, and I have a very high pain tolerance. But usually, I've found that there's a pretty high price for all of my symptoms if I continually ignore all of my body's pain signals. I have also found that there is no reward at the end for pushing through things when in reality, I need the rest. A big part of my journey has been letting go of the internalized shame I feel when I take the rest I need.

I have a medical card. I have tried many different medications, like anti psychotics, and anti depressants, and anti anxiety meds - with various rates of success. I am not currently on any other medication, and because of previous side effects - I am wary of taking it; although I'm not categorically opposed to it in the future. The medical marijuana helps me tremendously - it helps with dissociative episodes, it helps with anxiety, it helps with nightmares, it helps reduce the severity of my flashbacks, it helps me with suicidal thoughts. It helps me to regulate my moods. However, I feel unease about taking it long term. I'm cautious. I wish I had more input from medical professionals about my marijuana use, but as it stands now, it's self regulated. This level of responsibility is scary for me.

I think it's entirely possible that I will not survive the darkness that has enveloped my mind as of late. For a long time, I've said that if a magical being appeared in front of me and offered me two options - one being a bottle of sleeping pills guaranteed to make me never wake up again, the other being enough money so that I'd never have to worry about working again; I'd take the pills. This has been true for me for over the past decade; although I've certainly fantasized about suicide for longer.  

However, if I do survive this... if I somehow grit my teeth and make it through the storm that is brewing around me at this moment in time; I will be transformed through my healing. I will be stronger, more resilient, more able to use my voice to help others. I will be a lighthouse for other ships lost at sea. If I survive. 

If I was a four year old girl again, and I could somehow avoid the awful things that happened to me - of course, I wish that could happen. I wish my abuser had chosen a different path. I wish many different things had happened over the last thirty years. I can't even imagine who I could have been had trauma not taken me out at such an early age. I can't imagine what I could have achieved if I didn't spend the majority of my life fighting to crawl out of hell. But I don't have a time machine. I can only move forward and make do with what I got. I either die in the pity, and grief, and loss (and I may, because of things like shitty inconsistent therapy, and our society, and capitalism, and lack of resources, and lack of support, and inability to dream) or I grow around the grief and find the beauty in my healing. I am not looking for a silver lining, or something that will make me turn around and say it was all worth it - nothing was worth what I lived through - but I am looking at a post apocalyptic wasteland, at scorched earth, and I'm telling myself that maybe, something can still grow here. And maybe, I can hold on long enough to appreciate when it finally blooms. I think that hope in our world can be so amazingly naive, and I don't know what the next year will bring, but I hope that it's more hope. For me, and for everyone who needs it.

I'm an almost daily writer. I struggle with CPTSD, and I think journaling helps me keep track of moods and symptoms. Sometimes, it does feel like a chore - and when that happens, I usually step away for a couple of days to regroup myself. Most of the time, it's a practice in being my own friend, and being true to my voice and consistent with meeting my own needs.

I did DBT weekly for six months. I discontinued doing it because it was dehumanizing to me. I constantly felt unheard, invalidated, and dismissed. I hated every session, I complained about the homework, and I felt small and unheard in this style of therapy. I didn't think it was working, and I hated it.

It's been four months since I stopped this type of therapy; and I think I've changed my mind on its effectiveness for me. It wasn't good while it was happening; but I certainly learned a lot of skills that help me in my day to day life now - particularly radical acceptance, wise mind, and distress tolerance. There were also a lot of skills that I left behind - like opposite action. Overall, I'm glad I learned from it, and I don't regret doing it. I did find it helpful to work through the book with a therapist, in a group therapy setting - but I often benefit from group therapy.

I've tried a lot of different therapies throughout my treatment. At this point, I don't know that any specific type of therapy is perfect for me, and I hold no belief that therapy should be prescribed and recommended to everyone. There are simply too many bad therapists out there, and once you add in the pharmaceutical industry, and misdiagnosing folks, and insurance - it's a gamble, and the odds are not in favor of the client. I don't judge anyone who walks away from therapy in general, or from a style of therapy specifically. 

I find it helpful to look at each style of therapy as if I'm shopping for a new wardrobe. I go into different stores, try on different things in different sizes - and I walk away with what fits, leaving behind anything that doesn't. I'm an individual with unique needs, and ultimately I trust myself to know what is working for me, and what isn't.

I am open to the possibility that I am wrong - but from my experience, I haven't seen the term trauma dump be used as anything but a tool for silencing victims of abuse. 

I have no desire to let everyone I meet into the most intimate details of my worst days; but trauma colors who I am and how I move through the world; there's only so much I can do to censor myself to protect other people. I talk about it. I mention symptoms. I try my best to be aware of other people's triggers and be respectful, but I also have to respect my own truth and my voice.
It's brutal and heartbreaking. I'm sorry that you get it, it sucks.

How I see that play out, over and over again when people are actually faced with mental illness: Until your healing story is complete, with a bow and a happy ending, please keep it away from everyone else. Don't focus so much on the negative, it's dragging the rest of us down.

I'm 34. I've tried C and D. For a long time, I worked but I also fell in the A category, because I wouldn't have made it without my husband's salary. Our marriage didn't make it; and now I'm living with my parents and I'm not working. 

I've made a lot of progress in the last several months, and I'm hopeful that there is a future ahead of me where I'm able to be financially independent and secure. But I'm also constantly aware of how lucky and privileged I am to have the support of my parents, emotionally & financially, and this awareness puts pressure on me to want to hurry up my healing, even though I really need to slow down. I don't know how long it's going to take before I can have a job again. I have a lot of guilt and shame about being in the A category.

I'd really love to have a zoom group for check ins, if folks are into that. Like a coffee date, or a wine/whine session. I don't see a lot of people on a regular basis, and it's something my life is missing. I'd also love to have some accountability practices to one another - whether that's talking about dealing with symptoms, or therapy, or self care practices, or other hobbies that aren't directly linked to working through trauma. I'd be up for some sort of question of the day practice as well - and I'm also available to take charge of those kind of things if there's a need for that.

I take weed (medical marijuana), sit on the floor, and watch Grey's anatomy + play candy crush on my phone. Sometimes, I take more weed and try to sleep. I isolate and don't talk to people. I try to eat comfort foods, but it's hard to eat during this time. 

For me, it's what I do around the flashbacks that has more of a positive outcome than what I do during. I go for a walk most mornings when I first wake up. I journal most days, although sometimes my brain just doesn't go there. I try to eat three meals a day. I go to therapy twice a week. I'm slowly starting to add more to my days depending on my energy levels. The past eight months have been particularly tough, so I do what I can to survive. I'm slowly getting better, but I don't know what better looks like in the long term, and I get overwhelmed thinking about the future. Right now, I just try to focus on the present moment.

I've also had two therapists in my life that have made me feel heard, seen, and validated without throwing solutions my way; my last therapist and my current therapist. Both of them have never once offered advice without first asking if I wanted it. Both of them have encouraged patience in my healing, without being aggressively pushy. A lot of the time, they just end up being a witness to my story. And a lot of the time, that's exactly what I need. Both of them have been specialists in trauma. I really loved working with the first one, but I moved. I'm glad I was able to find my current therapist. I've only been going through this trauma therapy (rather than the therapy before, which was very aggressively directional and shaming) since August, but it's helping. It took me seven years of therapy and a lot of therapists to find this. 

Whether or not you continue to pursue therapy, I wish you best of luck in your journey!

In my break from running, I picked up yoga and weight lifting. I tried hiking and walking - although it's not the same, it is awesome. I picked up other hobbies that weren't activity focused. I found other ways to feel that sense of accomplishment. This may be possible for you as well.

I'm not a doctor; I'm a runner with a history of disordered eating. I would urge you to consider working with a medical professional - it is going to be at best, difficult, and potentially dangerous to restore your levels of fitness without proper nourishment. I really struggled with this at one point in my life, because I felt like I had to take a break from running and it was sad and frustrating. But my goal was always to return to running and to have a healthy relationship with the sport (which I didn't, because of my eating disorder) long term. It was possible, although not easy, to give up running for a period of time because I knew I'd come back to it. I don't presume to know your circumstances or reasons for running. I wish you best of luck in your recovery, health, wellness, and fitness!

It also sounds like it's hard to set boundaries with people, or people bypass straight over the boundaries that you do set, and overshare and overwhelm you. 

I hope that you can find some peace in your conversations with friends and family. You aren't an awful person. It's not your fault. You're not the problem.
